101.s: Creath's reputation and influence on later St. Louis trumpet players, though Terry never saw him.
101.q: No, because we had our own group. There’s a cat who – the Lord Mayor of the whole situation was a cat named Charlie Creath, spelled c-r-e-a-t-h, but he pronounced it Charlie Creth. He called himself the King of Cornet. Charlie Creath, King of Cornet. Now he could play, man. He could swing. He could…

101.t: Ham Davis and the St. Louis parades
101.s: Ham Davis played lead an octave higher marching through potholes; comparison with Reunald Jones.
101.q: Yeah, absolutely, on the part of everybody’s concept of trumpet playing and knowledge about trumpet playing, all passed on down through the line. Now one of the people who created another sort of a tradition, or thing associated with trumpet players, his name was Ham Davis, same like Miles Davis,…

101.t: Levi Madison and the Heim mouthpieces
101.s: Levi Madison's beautiful sound and odd practice habits, and Joe Gustave's students using Heim mouthpieces.
101.q: Levi Madison was a cat that we all loved so much, because he was the guy that we all felt, and still feel like, had the greatest trumpet sound of anybody in the world. But he’s a little bit poco loco, a little crazy. We used to sometimes check out lunches and go over to his apartment and stand…

101.t: The St. Louis trumpet sound: Creath, Gustave and the Heim mouthpiece
101.s: Terry agrees there is a St. Louis tradition stemming from Charlie Creath and Joe Gustave's students using Heims.
101.q: I think so, because most historians and people who keep up with the traditions of jazz from certain areas always refer to St. Louis trumpet players as a group of people who had a certain tradition, a certain sound, a certain background, because – and I think – I’ve been told that it all stems from…

859.t: Favourite trumpeters: Manuel Perez, Oliver, Keppard and Kid Rene
859.s: Gabriel prefers Manuel Perez, compares Perez, Oliver and Keppard, and Rene's tone.
859.ch: Trumpet players of the old days
859.q: Yeah, and another trumpet, you ask about trumpet players, I'm trying to think of one of them fellas used to jump up to old trumpet. I know these young fellas, I know you ain't trying to worry about them.

279.t: Cornet players, Bill Padron, Abbie Brunies and Louis Prima
279.s: Hug names favorite cornet players and recalls playing with Louis Prima at the Avalon Club.
279.q: Well, of course, the ones that I played with, I think I've already mentioned, like Bill Gillen and Bill Padron and Abbey Brunas. Let's see, Brent Bowman.

285.s: King Oliver, Manuel Perez, Freddie Keppard and Emil Christian were the trumpet players he heard coming up.
285.q: Yeah. Well, Louie came up after Joe went to Chicago, see. And, uh, when Manuel Perez played a sweet trumpet, nice, beautiful trumpet. But Joe could blast as high as the sky, see. Yeah. And Freddie Keppard could do the same. And the white boys, a kid by the name of Emil Christian. Oh, yeah.

977.t: Influences, King Oliver repertoire and favorite players
977.s: He was influenced by Rex Stewart, Bix and Armstrong, aimed for King Oliver's style, played first cornet with Luter, and names Oliver, Armstrong and others as favorites.
977.q: Oh, I'm not sure. I was, of course, influenced by the records I heard. Rex Stewart and Biggs Bayder Beck and Armstrong, of course.

296.t: Who was the best trumpet player; Perez and Oliver
296.s: Pressed to judge Perez against Joe Oliver, he declines and says both were good; session winds down.
296.q: yeah they both was good mm-hmm name some of them name some of them when Perez went and went to Chicago uh Joe Oliver took his job uh here in town

715.s: Allen praises Charlie Creath's tone and blues playing, his bands around St. Louis, the Zutty Singleton family tie, and his death.
715.q: I don't know. I think he recorded years in St. Louis. Okay people went around to different cities around that time and used to take their equipment and have their local fans record. I think he recorded a lot. And after he was in Chicago I don't know whether he didn't record or not. But at that time…

783.t: Charlie Creath's trumpet tone and the St. Louis style
783.s: Asked about the St. Louis style, Shoffner praises Creath's blues playing and solid concert tone.
783.q: Well, he was really top-zone blues and he had a good tone. He was one of the few jazz trumpet players that had a good, what we call a concert tone, a good solid tone. I see, of course, you know, during that time, you know, during the daytime, or, uh, Dway Jackson had the band on that same boat.…

641.t: Mutt's bragging; Kid Thomas and Keppard compared
641.s: Joe says Mutt boasted constantly, then Barry and Joe compare Kid Thomas, Freddie Keppard and Kid Rena.
641.ch: Los Angeles with Mutt Carey and the taxi dances
641.q: Oh, Mutt thought he was the greatest thing in the world, if you listened to him. He was the braggin'est you ever seen in your life! One of these

76.t: Northern popular style and Creath's blues
76.s: Creath's band played northern stock orchestrations in the style of Isham Jones and Paul Whiteman, not New Orleans style, but Creath was famed as a soulful blues player.
76.ch: Chicago, the Marable boats and Marge's St. Louis family band
76.q: And of course you had to read because we have these little orchestrations, we have to play popular music. We weren't playing the New Orleans style of jazz, you know. We were playing the northern style, like, you know, and Charlie and Mark, Ishon Jones and --

79.t: Charlie Creath's sound and sharp dress
79.s: Thomas praises Charlie Creath's individual trumpet sound and his dapper pongee shirts. Creath worked the riverboats.
79.ch: Trumpet teachers and St. Louis heroes
79.q: He sounded like Charlie Creath [SINGS]. And the chicks would run and jump on the boats behind him. He was tremendous.
